objective: Configuring Windows security settings: Windows Defender/Firewall, BitLocker, and User Account Control
secondaryObjectives: Logical security concepts: least privilege, multifactor authentication, ACLs, and encryption
Securing mobile and embedded devices: screen locks, remote wipe, and full-device encryption

sources.cite: CompTIA A+ Core 2 (220-1202) V15 Exam Objectives, Document Version 4.0: domains Operating systems 28%, Security 28%, Software troubleshooting 23%, Operational procedures 21%; launched 2025-03-25
sources.note: Objective 2.6 'Given a scenario, implement procedures for basic small office/home office (SOHO) malware removal', read in primary text in the objectives PDF on 2026-11-14: '1. Investigate and verify malware symptoms. 2. Quarantine infected system. 3. Disable System Restore in Windows Home. 4. Remediate infected systems. 5. Update anti-malware software. 6. Scan and removal techniques (e.g., safe mode, preinstallation environment) 7. Reimage/reinstall. 8. Schedule scans and run updates. 9. Enable System Restore and create a restore point in Windows Home. 10. Educate the end user.' Objective 3.4 lists 'False alerts regarding antivirus protection', 'Random/frequent pop-ups' and 'Redirection'. The exam page (summarizing fetch, same day) gives the domains and launch date. Reused for REQ-336 from this course's home-office-laptop-malware (the same reading and date); the objective wording is the course seed's.

The business, the users, the devices and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You are the IT technician at Fenwick Supplies, a fictional distributor. A sales rep's laptop was stolen from a car last week; it held a customer price list. The owner wants the other twelve sales laptops secured this week.
handover: The laptops run Windows Pro with TPM 2.0; BitLocker is off on all of them.
Sales reps are local administrators; two turned UAC off because prompts annoyed them.
howItWorks: The desk shows the ticket queue against the priority matrix and each service's status.
Move on a ticket round at a time. A decision comes to you at each ticket round; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Round 2: a firmware update triggers BitLocker recovery on three laptops; their keys are inside the locked drives and the reps lose a day.
Round 3: a rep opens a fake invoice; with UAC off and admin rights, it installs a keylogger silently.
Round 4: on a trade-show network, another attendee's infected laptop reaches the reps' shared folders.

choices.label: Enable BitLocker with the TPM on each laptop, back up each recovery key to the company account (not the laptop itself), and confirm encryption completes

effects.log: Twelve laptops encrypted; recovery keys escrowed.

choices.feedback: Full-disk encryption protects a stolen laptop's data; an escrowed recovery key lets IT unlock it when the TPM can't.

choices.label: Encrypt the four laptops that hold price lists
choices.feedback: The others hold customer data too.

choices.label: Enable BitLocker and save each recovery key to a text file on the laptop's desktop

effects.log: Recovery keys are saved on each laptop.

choices.feedback: A recovery key on the encrypted laptop is no use when you need it, and on a USB stick in the bag it unlocks the thief's copy.

uacPrompt.title: Admin rights and UAC
uacPrompt.context: Reps install a CRM plug-in a few times a year.

choices.label: Make the reps standard users, keep a separate admin account for IT, and turn UAC back on at the default level

effects.log: Reps are standard users; UAC is on.

choices.feedback: Least privilege: malware running as a standard user can't install drivers or change system settings, and UAC prompts for elevation.

choices.label: Turn UAC back on but leave reps as administrators
choices.feedback: Better, but a click on 'Yes' still gives malware full rights.

choices.label: Leave UAC off so reps aren't interrupted
choices.feedback: Everything a rep runs, including malware, runs with full rights silently.

fwPrompt.title: Firewall off on hotel Wi-Fi
fwPrompt.context: The old VPN client complained; the current one works with the firewall on.

choices.label: Turn Windows Defender Firewall on for all profiles and add a specific allow rule for the current VPN client only if it needs one

effects.log: The firewall is on everywhere; the VPN works.

choices.feedback: The public profile matters most on hotel and café Wi-Fi; a specific rule beats turning the firewall off.

choices.label: Turn it on for the domain and private profiles only
choices.feedback: Public Wi-Fi is exactly where the reps need it.

choices.label: Turn the firewall off on all twelve so the VPN never complains
choices.feedback: Every laptop's file sharing and services are exposed on every network.

reflection.question: Write the work notes for the owner: what a thief or malware could have done before, and what each setting now prevents.

scoring.modelReasoning: BitLocker with a TPM encrypts the whole drive so a stolen laptop's data is unreadable; the recovery key must be escrowed with the organization. Least privilege means standard user accounts with UAC prompting for elevation, so malware can't install silently. Windows Defender Firewall should be on for every profile, especially public, with specific rules rather than turning it off.
